terms.comment: The adjective of oriēns, the east (see east): post-classical (Justin, Gellius), but the plain word, and Augustine’s for the Christians of the East. Classical prose has no adjective for it and says it with the noun.

evidence: Cic. N.D. 2.66: ab oriente ad occidentem (Lewis & Short, s.v. orior)
terms.comment: The classical way: ad orientem spectāre, to face east, as Cato’s in merīdiem spectet for south (see southern); quae ad orientem sunt, the eastern parts.

phrases.latin: tunc hymnī et psalmī ut canerentur secundum mōrem orientālium partium, nē populus maerōris taediō contābēsceret, īnstitūtum est
phrases.english: it was then laid down that hymns and psalms should be sung after the custom of the eastern regions, so that the people should not waste away in weary grief

sources: Lewis & Short: orientalis · Lewis & Short: orior
